title: Make generation earn another attempt
standfirst: The shortest route stopped at a rack. The warmest ending promised a day we had not built.

blocks.title: The winner at the loading dock
blocks.caption: Inspecting a proposal does not promote it: the paper cards track your inspection, while the result slip keeps the evaluator’s selection visible.

blocks.text: Start with proposal A and keep considering the next one. Under the distance-only rule, the selected route becomes shorter. At the seventh proposal, the score has fallen from twelve grid units to six. Try that winner. The cargo stops at the central rack. The chart we could have drawn from those scores would slope in the direction we wanted, all the way to a failed delivery.

I held the destinations and the loaded cart’s footprint fixed, then let the first ranking rule ignore clearance. The failure cannot be blamed on a moving target. Requiring clear delivery changes the winner; closing the door brings back a longer route that was available at the beginning. Another batch of proposals would have been less useful than repairing what selection was allowed to notice. This is an authored collection, not an estimate of a model’s discovery rate.
Give computation an outcome it can improve

Richard Sutton’s 2019 Bitter Lesson argues that general methods able to absorb more computation have repeatedly overtaken elaborate stores of human domain knowledge. Search and learning are central to that history. I take the ambition seriously: a system should be able to benefit from another thousand attempts. But the essay does not make our local score a reliable definition of success. Scaling the wrong selection rule remains our responsibility.

blocks.alt: Published FunSearch Figure 1. A specification and sampled programs form a prompt; a pretrained language model proposes programs, evaluation filters them, and a programs database feeds later prompts.
blocks.caption: Romera-Paredes and colleagues, Figure 1, published December 2023, CC BY 4.0. The retained program is both an output and material for another proposal. Original figure, resized and re-encoded; inspect for the individual paths.

blocks.text: FunSearch makes an important choice about what gets generated. Bernardino Romera-Paredes and colleagues search for programs that construct solutions, pairing a pretrained language model with an evaluator. A stable program skeleton can leave a critical decision function open to change. Their cap-set and bin-packing results concern problems with useful executable evaluation; they do not establish a general machine for deciding whether generated work is good.

The executable program matters because it can be tried again under a changed condition. Our tiny route policies choose a row through the yard; closing the door asks a new question of the same candidate. That makes the proposal more useful than a persuasive account of a successful delivery. It also creates evaluation work every time we expand the conditions the result must survive.

AlphaEvolve extends this pattern to code modifications, evaluated candidates and an evolving population. Its optional evaluation cascade rejects weak proposals before more expensive stages; its database balances exploiting strong candidates with retaining diversity. The authors also allow model-generated judgments for qualities that are harder to specify. Those judgments enter as evaluation choices, not independent truth. The paper’s strongest applicability claim remains tied to machine-gradeable solutions.

blocks.title: The route we almost threw away
blocks.caption: A and B both remain feasible when the doorway closes. Their twelve-unit tie is settled alphabetically; retaining alternatives does not require pretending that every one is uniquely best.

blocks.text: Keeping E alone is economical until the doorway closes. The drawer then contains no feasible answer. Retaining A and B buys options under the changed requirement, at the cost of storing and reconsidering more than a single winner. The lesson is selective retention, not an obligation to keep every near-duplicate forever. This desk illustrates the decision; it does not reproduce AlphaEvolve’s evolving population.

Andrej Karpathy’s March 2026 autoresearch repository makes a compact version of this boundary legible. The agent changes a training file; a separate preparation file contains fixed evaluation and constants. Experiments receive a five-minute training budget, excluding startup and compilation, and compare validation bits per byte. The instructions forbid changing the evaluation harness. The README also limits comparability across different hardware. This is a disciplined experimental envelope, not evidence that five minutes is the right horizon for a game or any other project.
Candidate improvement and evaluator improvement deserve separate records. If a missing condition changes the judge, rerun the baseline and retained alternatives before enlarging search.

Visual Artist’s night-image review needed another kind of selection. The first candidate lost continuity with the entrance; the revision restored the slogan and right-hand barrel. Full-image containment and a narrow-width inspection followed. The useful feedback named a visible omission. An invented scalar for “the same factory after everyone has left” would have made the comparison look more mechanical without making it more dependable.

Once clearance rejects the straight route, six more near-identical paths through the rack teach us little. A different corridor, footprint or obstruction hypothesis could be worth a trial. I would make that question explicit before buying the next batch. Evaluation and review are part of the generation system’s cost; the productive unit is a comparison that can change what we keep.

blocks.title: Make the next trial informative
blocks.body: Begin with a bounded candidate family and an evaluator that can reject a tempting shortcut. The yard’s geometry and rankings are computed locally; no model account is needed.
steps: Keep the world rules fixed. Write a candidate that passes, a shorter candidate that violates a requirement, and a valid alternative that survives a second operating condition.
Compute feasibility separately from the quantity being optimized. Preserve the exact candidate and evaluator version with each result.
Try a cheap rejection stage before a costly integrated trial. Confirm that the early stage does not discard the alternative needed for the second condition.
Retain the baseline and distinct useful alternatives. If a reviewer changes an acceptance condition, rerun that small collection before expanding generation.
blocks.exercise: Only replace the fixed proposal list with model-generated route code after the evaluator is dependable. Keep execution isolated and set a trial budget. Before another batch, state which unresolved question it could answer and which result would make you stop.

blocks.text: A new line is not always a new scene

blocks.title: An hour before the gate closes
blocks.caption: The exit requires the period to be spent, not the characters to agree. An unanswered request and an honoured one can therefore close the same scene.

blocks.text: Kit wants a rehearsal. Lou can ask, make space for it, and leave with an invitation to try again tomorrow. Or Lou can spend the hour making another crate. The exit is the same door. The person walking through it has a different reason to speak.

I nearly gave this miniature a revealing omission. I had added “wants quiet” as a second intention, guarded the rehearsal against that request, and left production as the only way to finish the period. Kit could refuse the activity I preferred, but could not get the thing they had asked for. I caught the missing response while enumerating the scene’s branches and added a quiet beat. It was a writing error expressed as a perfectly serviceable set of controls.

The repaired scene spends one period on a request and an activity. Its three rehearsal endings interpret the same history without awarding a relationship point. They can add rhythm, implication or character, which may be valuable. They do not add three new outcomes. That distinction matters when a generator offers an impressive pile of apparent variety.

Emily Short’s definition of a storylet joins content to prerequisites and effects. The content may be dialogue, prose, animation or film; the definition leaves its size and selection method open. Her 2019 essay shows how this small structure can express several familiar narrative shapes. What I find useful here is the obligation hidden inside its apparent simplicity: specify when this passage belongs, and what is different after it.

Our rehearsal requires an unspent period and an expressed wish to practise. Another writer or model can improve Kit’s line without gaining permission to restore the hour or invent a promise. A genuinely different consequence costs more: its prerequisites must be reachable, its effect must be stored, and later scenes must respect it. Fluency does not pay those obligations on our behalf.

Failbetter’s 2012 StoryNexus diary explains why this arrangement helps a team add material: contributors agree on the state changes they may make. It also admits that the repeated setup–choice–result rhythm can make longer dramatic scenes awkward. Both observations matter. Small units offer useful boundaries, but a boundary that makes collaboration convenient can interrupt the experience it is supposed to carry.

The studio Writer’s cohort proposal improved when Theatre stopped conferring an automatic benefit: Lou would ask what Kit wanted, Sam would have a say, and practice would compete with output. It remained authored source, not a Day 1 result. That correction inspired this teaching scene. It gives Short’s conditions-and-effects model a concrete application, while leaving any claim about improved player experience unmeasured.
The next scene receives the bill

blocks.title: What the last line smuggles in
blocks.caption: If the booking is meant to be true, accepting that line creates work for a later scene: an appointment needs somewhere to happen, and some way to be missed.

blocks.text: A warm line can quietly appoint tomorrow’s rehearsal, imply everybody enjoyed today’s, or promise a resource the world does not have. If those implications are intentional, the design needs to support them. If they are accidental, accepting the line creates repair work downstream. I want the scene record beside the alternatives so a beautiful sentence cannot revise the commission unnoticed.

Façade joins reactive behavior and a drama manager to authored material. Mateas and Stern’s later authoring account shows the cost in a dispute over drinks: interruption points, topic recovery, repeated requests and physical staging had to be specified around the lines. They report substantial local responsiveness alongside less global agency than hoped, with joint dialogue behavior still costly to write. The architecture made that work possible without removing it.

I ended this miniature’s responsibility at the gate and made its final beat indivisible. An interruptible rehearsal would need separate start and completion states, then endings for abandonment or return. That could be worth adding if interruption becomes a consequential player action. More interchangeable closing lines would not implement it. The next commission should name which kind of richness it is buying.

Bruno Dias’s account of trying to generalize Voyageur’s narrative machinery provides a useful builder’s counterweight. He separates narrative selection, text generation and the interface, then describes how the small dynamic portion of otherwise static storylets carried much of their value. His general-purpose project stalled over scope and tooling compromises. This is not a warning against reusable tools. It is evidence that a format convenient for one game does not automatically become a good authoring system for many.

blocks.title: Author one return to a shared place
blocks.body: Give the small factory a scene that comes back to the same location after different earlier actions.
steps: Write two histories that reach the same doorway. State exactly which earlier fact makes the ending differ.
Give every scene a prerequisite and an explicit effect. Include one refusal that the system can honour rather than merely display.
Separate alternate wording from alternate consequences. Inspect whether any line invents a commitment absent from the record.
Enumerate the reachable histories. Try each one through the actual presentation, including a request the preferred activity cannot satisfy.
blocks.exercise: Generate three variations of one eligible passage with the effects held fixed. Compare what each adds to the scene. Then propose one genuinely different consequence and list the later work it creates; decide whether that difference is worth implementing.
